claims.text: Demanding mechanical loading can induce phase separation or precipitation in HEAs initially designed as single-phase solid solutions.
The service-induced secondary phases may include brittle intermetallics or carbides.
Secondary brittle phases act as crack-initiation sites.
Formation of secondary brittle phases reduces toughness and can lead to brittle fracture.
Elevated temperature or cyclic loading can destabilize the initially single-phase microstructure.
Secondary phases form at grain boundaries or within grains and cause embrittlement.
Mechanical and/or thermal energy during service drives atomic diffusion.
Service-driven atomic diffusion causes phase instability and precipitation of brittle phases.
Brittle secondary phases reduce the alloy's ability to accommodate plastic deformation.
Reduced plastic accommodation promotes crack initiation and propagation.
After service exposure, fracture toughness or Charpy impact energy will decrease relative to the as-prepared single-phase baseline.
After service exposure, fracture mode will transition from ductile to brittle.
Microstructural analysis after service exposure will reveal secondary-phase formation.
The as-prepared single-phase HEA has high toughness and ductile fracture behavior.
The proposed behavior applies when temperature and stress are sufficient to drive phase instability but not under mild conditions or in exceptionally phase-stable alloys.
